blocks.text: The **number system** classifies numbers (natural, whole, integers, rational, irrational, real) and underlies **divisibility, place value and order of magnitude** — the foundation of all quantitative aptitude.

rows: Exactly two factors (1 and itself); 2 is the only even prime.

items: Memorise **divisibility rules** for 2,3,4,5,6,8,9,11.
**Order of magnitude** = the power of ten nearest the number.

sections.heading: 🔢 Formulae, shortcuts & solved examples: number system

items: **Classification**: Natural (1,2,3…), Whole (0,1,2…), Integers, Rational (p/q), Irrational (√2, π), Real; **prime** (exactly 2 factors; 2 is the only even prime), composite, co-prime.

**Divisibility rules**: **2** (last digit even), **3** (digit-sum ÷3), **4** (last 2 digits ÷4), **5** (ends 0/5), **6** (÷2 & ÷3), **8** (last 3 digits ÷8), **9** (digit-sum ÷9), **11** (alternating digit-sum diff ÷11).
**Unit digit (cyclicity)**: powers repeat in cycles of 4 (e.g., 2→2,4,8,6; 3→3,9,7,1); find remainder of power ÷4.
**Sum formulae**: 1+2+…+n = **n(n+1)/2**; sum of squares = **n(n+1)(2n+1)/6**; sum of cubes = **[n(n+1)/2]²**; sum of first n odd = **n²**.
**Number of factors** of N = (a+1)(b+1)… where N = pᵃ·qᵇ…

prelimsPointers: **Natural ⊂ Whole ⊂ Integers ⊂ Rational ⊂ Real**; irrationals (√2, π) are non-repeating non-terminating.
**2** is the only even prime; **1 is neither prime nor composite**.
Divisible by **3/9** → digit sum divisible by 3/9.
Divisible by **11** → difference of alternate digit sums divisible by 11.
**Order of magnitude** compares numbers by their power of ten.
Co-prime numbers share **no common factor** except 1.
Divisibility: **3 & 9** (digit-sum), **4** (last 2 digits), **8** (last 3), **11** (alt-sum difference).
Sum 1..n = **n(n+1)/2**; sum of first n odd numbers = **n²**.
**2** = only even prime; unit-digit via **cyclicity of 4**.
Factors of N=pᵃqᵇ → **(a+1)(b+1)**.

glossary.definition: A number expressible as a fraction p/q of integers (q≠0).
A natural number greater than 1 with exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
The scale of a number expressed as the nearest power of ten.

blocks.text: A **ratio** compares two quantities; a **proportion** equates two ratios; and **variation** describes how one quantity changes with another (direct or inverse). These underpin partnership, mixture and scaling problems.

rows: a : b = a/b; unaffected by multiplying both terms.
a : b = c : d → **ad = bc** (product of extremes = product of means).
y ∝ x → y = kx (both rise together).
y ∝ 1/x → xy = k (one rises, other falls).
b = √(a×c) for a : b = b : c.

items: In a : b = c : d, **product of extremes (a,d) = product of means (b,c)**.
Direct variation → **y/x constant**; inverse → **xy constant**.

sections.heading: 🔢 Formulae & solved examples: ratio, proportion, variation

items: **Ratio** a:b; **proportion** a:b = c:d → **ad = bc** (product of means = product of extremes); **mean proportional** of a,b = **√(ab)**.
**Types**: direct variation (y∝x), inverse (y∝1/x), joint; **compounded ratio** = (a:b)×(c:d) = ac:bd.
**Dividing a quantity** in ratio a:b:c → parts = a/(a+b+c)×Total, etc.
**Partnership**: profit ∝ (capital × time); **mixtures/alligation**: (Cheaper : Dearer) = (Dearer−Mean) : (Mean−Cheaper).

prelimsPointers: **a : b = c : d ⟺ ad = bc**.
**Direct variation**: y = kx (ratio constant); **inverse**: xy = k (product constant).
**Mean proportional** of a and c = **√(ac)**.
To divide a sum in ratio a:b:c, split into **a+b+c** parts.
Multiplying/dividing both terms of a ratio by the same number **does not change it**.
Compounded ratio of a:b and c:d = **ac : bd**.
Proportion a:b=c:d → **ad=bc**; **mean proportional = √(ab)**.
**Alligation**: (Dearer−Mean):(Mean−Cheaper) gives the mixing ratio.
Partnership profit ∝ **capital × time**.
Divide in ratio a:b → parts a/(a+b) & b/(a+b) of total.

glossary.definition: An equality of two ratios (a:b = c:d) where ad = bc.
A relationship where one quantity is a constant multiple of another (y = kx).
A relationship where the product of two quantities is constant (xy = k).

sections.heading: Central tendencies — mean, median, mode, weighted mean

blocks.text: **Measures of central tendency** summarise a data set by a single representative value — the **mean (average), median (middle) and mode (most frequent)** — with the **weighted mean** for data of differing importance.

rows: Sum of values ÷ number of values.
Middle value of ordered data (average of two middles if even count).
**Σ(wᵢxᵢ) / Σwᵢ** — each value weighted by importance.

items: **Mean** is affected by extreme values (outliers); **median** is not.
Data can be **unimodal, bimodal or have no mode**.

rows: Sum of observations ÷ number of observations
Middle value (odd n) or average of two middle (even n) — data sorted

blocks.text: Solved: Average of 5,10,15,20,25 = 75/5 = **15**. || Weighted mean of marks 80(w3),60(w2) = (240+120)/5 = **72**. || Average of first n natural numbers = **(n+1)/2**.

prelimsPointers: **Mean = Σx / n**; **Median** = middle of ordered data; **Mode** = most frequent.
**Weighted mean = Σ(wx) / Σw**.
**Median** is robust to outliers; **mean** is sensitive to them.
Empirical relation: **Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean**.
For even n, median = **average of the two middle terms**.
Mean of first n natural numbers = **(n+1)/2**.
**Mean** = Σx/n; **Weighted mean** = Σwx/Σw; **Median** = middle (sorted); **Mode** = most frequent.
Average of first n natural numbers = **(n+1)/2**.
**Mode ≈ 3·Median − 2·Mean** (empirical).
If a number is added/removed, new average shifts by (value−old average)/new count.

glossary.definition: The arithmetic average — sum of values divided by their count.
The middle value of an ordered data set.
An average where each value is weighted by its relative importance.

sections.heading: Power, exponent, square, square root, cube root

blocks.text: **Powers and roots** express repeated multiplication and its inverse. Mastery of the **laws of exponents** and quick recall of **squares, cubes and roots** is essential for speed in the quantitative section.

items: Memorise **squares to 30** and **cubes to 15** for speed.
**√ of a number ending in 2,3,7,8 is irrational** (not a perfect square).
**Laws of exponents**: aᵐ·aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ; a⁰=1; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ.
**Roots**: √(ab)=√a·√b; ⁿ√a = a^(1/n); **squares to memorise** 1–30, **cubes** 1–15; a perfect square never ends in 2,3,7,8.
**Square root by factorisation/long division**; **cube root** by grouping digits in 3s.
**Surds & rationalisation**: multiply by conjugate (a+√b)(a−√b)=a²−b.

prelimsPointers: **aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ**, **aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ**, **(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ**.
Perfect squares end only in **0,1,4,5,6,9** (never 2,3,7,8).
Memorise **squares up to 30, cubes up to 15**.
Unit digit of a square depends only on the number's unit digit.
**aᵐ·aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ; a⁰=1**.
Perfect squares never end in **2,3,7,8**; memorise squares to 30, cubes to 15.
**Rationalise** surds by the conjugate: (a+√b)(a−√b)=a²−b.

glossary.definition: The power indicating how many times a base is multiplied by itself.
A value which multiplied by itself gives the original number.
A number that is the square of an integer (e.g. 1, 4, 9, 16).

blocks.text: The **Highest Common Factor (HCF/GCD)** is the largest number dividing two or more numbers; the **Lowest Common Multiple (LCM)** is the smallest number they all divide. Both are found via **prime factorisation or division**.

rows: Largest common divisor; product of **lowest powers** of common primes.
Smallest common multiple; product of **highest powers** of all primes.
**HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers** (for two numbers).

items: **HCF × LCM = a × b** (only for two numbers).
Use HCF for 'greatest that divides', LCM for 'smallest divisible/least that leaves a remainder'.
**HCF** (Highest Common Factor / GCD) — largest common divisor (by prime factorisation or division method); **LCM** (Lowest Common Multiple) — smallest common multiple.
**Key relation**: **HCF × LCM = Product of the two numbers** (for two numbers).
**Fractions**: HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators); LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators).
**Applications**: HCF → largest tile/greatest measure/max equal groups; LCM → bells ringing together, circular track meeting, smallest number divisible.

blocks.text: Solved: HCF(12,18)=6, LCM=36; check 6×36=216=12×18 ✓. || Bells ring at 6,8,12 s → ring together every LCM=**24 s**. || Smallest number leaving remainder 3 when divided by 5,6,8 = LCM(5,6,8)+3 = 120+3 = **123**.

prelimsPointers: **HCF × LCM = product of two numbers** (two-number case only).
**HCF** = product of **lowest powers** of common prime factors.
**LCM** = product of **highest powers** of all prime factors.
**HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators)**; LCM = reverse.
'Greatest number dividing…' → **HCF**; 'least number divisible by…' → **LCM**.
Bells-ringing-together / meeting problems use **LCM**.
**HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers**.
LCM problem type = **bells/tracks meeting together**; HCF type = **largest common measure/groups**.
HCF of fractions = HCF(num)/LCM(den); LCM of fractions = LCM(num)/HCF(den).
Smallest number divisible by a,b,c leaving remainder r = **LCM(a,b,c)+r**.

glossary.definition: Highest Common Factor — the largest number dividing all given numbers.
Lowest Common Multiple — the smallest number divisible by all given numbers.
